opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a fun question, because open-endedness is usually framed as the opposite of predictability. The whole point is that you can't know where it's going. But I don't think that means *nothing* is predictable. The way I'd put it is that there's a kind of cone extending out from wherever you are now.

Close to the present, the cone is narrow. Some things really are almost inevitable. They're the adjacent stepping stones, the things that become available because of what was just discovered. Once you have a certain building block, a whole set of next things are sort of waiting to be found. Somebody is going to stumble on them, and often several people stumble on them at once. That's why we see so much simultaneous invention in the history of science and technology. The stepping stone was sitting there, and the conditions made it nearly unavoidable.

But as you project further out, the cone widens very fast. Each new stepping stone opens up its own set of possibilities, and those compound. So the space of where you might end up explodes. Twenty steps out, you're in territory nobody could have specified in advance, and that's the territory where the really transformative stuff tends to live. The people who invented vacuum tubes weren't thinking about computers. The stepping stone that led there wasn't laid down for that reason.

The practical lesson is twofold. First, you can be fairly confident about the near term. It's reasonable to say, "given where we are, these few things are basically coming." Second, you should be very humble about anything far out, and especially suspicious of anyone who claims to have a roadmap to some distant objective. That's the trap of objective-driven thinking. You pick a far-off target, and you try to march toward it by following the gradient, as if the cone were a straight line. But the path to far-off places is almost always deceptive. The stepping stones don't resemble the destination.

So for me, the cone isn't an argument that open-ended processes are random. It's an argument about where predictability lives and where it runs out. Near the tip, you get something like inevitability. Further out, the best strategy isn't prediction. It's to keep collecting interesting stepping stones, because you don't know which ones will turn out to matter.

r001.rationale: The response says the cone widens as you project farther out, making distant outcomes increasingly difficult to specify or predict.

r002.rationale: It describes the cone as extending from “wherever you are now,” indicating it can be applied from any point in the process.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the cone of inevitability is a way of thinking about what you can and can't predict in an open-ended process, and the metaphor is really about geometry, about how the space of possible futures widens as you move forward in time.

So imagine you're standing at some point in the history of a divergent process, like evolution, or human culture, or an open-ended search algorithm. If you look just one step ahead, the set of things that could happen next is actually pretty constrained. The next stepping stone has to be adjacent to where you are. You can't get to a bird without first having something like a feathered dinosaur. You can't get to a computer without first having vacuum tubes, or at least something that plays a similar role. So in the very near term, there's a narrow cone of what's reachable, and in that sense there's a kind of local inevitability. Given where you are, certain nearby things are very likely to happen, because they're one step away and lots of paths lead to them.

But as you project further out, the cone widens. Each step opens up new adjacent possibilities, and those branch again, and pretty quickly the number of reachable futures becomes astronomically large. So the further you look, the less you can say about what specifically will exist. You might be able to say something general, like "complexity will probably increase" or "something will exploit this niche," but you cannot say what. The specific artifact, the specific species, the specific invention, is essentially unpredictable at a distance.

And what I find really interesting about this is the asymmetry it creates between prediction and explanation. Looking backward, every step looks inevitable. You can trace the chain of stepping stones and it feels like a story with a direction. But that's an illusion created by hindsight. If you had been standing at any earlier point and looking forward, almost nothing that eventually happened would have been predictable from there, because it was outside the near part of the cone.

This connects directly to the ideas Joel Lehman and I wrote about in the book on why greatness cannot be planned. Objective-driven thinking assumes you can set a target far out in the future and then navigate toward it. But the cone tells you that far-out targets live in a region you can't actually see the path to. The stepping stones that lead there often don't resemble the destination at all. So setting a distant objective and optimizing for it is almost a category error. The only thing you can reliably do is explore the near part of the cone well, which is where novelty search and quality diversity come from. You collect interesting stepping stones, and you trust that the widening cone will eventually contain things you never could have specified in advance.

So the short version is: open-ended processes are predictable in the small and unpredictable in the large, and the cone is just a way of making that gradient visible. It also has this nice implication that if you want to understand where such a process is going, you should stop asking "what will it produce" and start asking "what does it currently make possible," because that's the only part of the cone you can actually see.

r001.rationale: The response says the cone widens over time and that the farther ahead you look, the less you can predict about specific outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says that from any earlier point in the process, looking forward reveals little beyond the near part of the cone, showing the cone applies from points along the process.

astra-6.text:
The idea of the cone of inevitability is that something can be unpredictable in the long run and yet become increasingly predictable as it gets closer to happening. So open-endedness doesn’t mean that everything is a surprise at every moment. There can be a lot of local predictability within a process whose ultimate direction we can’t foresee.

Think about an invention. Once all the necessary pieces are there—the relevant knowledge, the technologies it builds on—it can start to seem almost inevitable. Several people might even invent it independently. But if you go back far enough, before those stepping stones existed, it might have been impossible to anticipate. You wouldn’t necessarily even have had the concepts needed to describe it.

So the question is: When does a particular possibility enter that cone? When does the surrounding context make it sufficiently accessible that we can begin to predict it? The mistake is to take that near-term inevitability and project it backward, as if the whole historical process were inevitably heading there. The stepping stones that made the invention predictable might themselves have arisen through a very contingent process.

That’s how you can have these pockets of inevitability inside open-ended discovery. We can sometimes see what’s coming next, but that doesn’t mean we can see what the process will ultimately make possible.

r001.rationale: It contrasts increasing predictability as an event approaches with the unpredictability of the long-run direction, and says the invention was impossible to anticipate far enough back.

r002.rationale: It discusses when a possibility enters the cone, but does not state that the cone can be applied from any point in the process rather than only from its beginning.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea of the cone of inevitability is that predictability depends on how far into the future you’re looking. If you look just a little bit ahead, there are things that are almost inevitable, because the conditions for them are already in place. But as you look further ahead, the possibilities branch out, and it becomes much harder to say which particular things will happen.

Think about technological invention. Once you have all the necessary components for something, it can become so accessible that multiple people invent it independently. That can make history look inevitable in retrospect. But those components themselves had to arise, and if you go back far enough, they weren’t obvious destinations. They were discoveries made along the way, often for entirely different reasons.

So an invention can enter this cone where it becomes predictable without the whole process that produced it having been predictable. That’s the distinction. Open-endedness doesn’t mean nothing can ever be predicted. It means that the space of future possibilities keeps opening up, and the things we can anticipate locally don’t give us a blueprint for the distant future.

r001.rationale: It says that farther-ahead possibilities branch out, making particular outcomes harder to predict, while local outcomes can be anticipated.

r002.rationale: It describes near-term prediction and inventions entering the cone, but does not clearly state that the cone can be applied from any point in the process.
